questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / Photon energy and the wave-particle picture
questions.stem: A sodium street lamp glows with light of frequency $5.1 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Take the Planck constant as $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$. One photon of this light carries an energy of
questions.solution:
A photon's energy is fixed by its frequency alone:
$$E=hf.$$

Substitute:
$$E=(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(5.1 \times 10^{14})=3.4 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

Work the powers of ten separately if it helps: $6.63 \times 5.1 \approx 34$, and $10^{-34} \times 10^{14}=10^{-20}$, giving $34 \times 10^{-20}=3.4 \times 10^{-19}$.

A few times $10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$ is the right size for visible light — about $2\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is why visible photons can just about dislodge electrons from some metals.
distractorRationale: Doubled the result, as though two photons were involved. The question asks about one.
Halved the result. Brightness sets how many photons arrive; frequency alone sets the energy of each.
Divided $h$ by the frequency instead of multiplying. Higher frequency means a more energetic photon, so frequency belongs on the top.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / Photon energy and the wave-particle picture
questions.stem: A laser pointer emits green light of wavelength $500\ \mathrm{nm}$. Take $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$ and $c=3.0 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. The energy of one photon is
questions.solution:
The frequency is not given, so eliminate it using $c=f\lambda$:
$$E=hf=\frac{hc}{\lambda}.$$

**Convert the wavelength first.** A nanometre is $10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$, so
$$\lambda=500\ \mathrm{nm}=5.00 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}.$$

**Substitute.**
$$E=\frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3.0 \times 10^{8})}{5.00 \times 10^{-7}}=\frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{5.00 \times 10^{-7}}=3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$
distractorRationale: This is $hc$ on its own — the division by the wavelength was never carried out.
Correct. $E=hc/\lambda=3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.
Used $250\ \mathrm{nm}$, halving the wavelength and so doubling the energy.
Left the wavelength as the bare number $500$ instead of converting to metres, losing nine powers of ten.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / Photon energy and the wave-particle picture
questions.stem: Which observation is explained by treating light as a stream of separate energy packets, rather than as a continuous wave?
options: $\text{Bright and dark fringes from a pair of narrow slits}$
$\text{Light spreading out after passing a narrow gap}$
$\text{Electrons ejected from a metal the instant light of a high enough frequency arrives}$
$\text{A beam bending as it enters a block of glass}$
questions.solution:
Three of these are wave behaviour, and the wave model handles them comfortably: fringes are interference, spreading past a gap is diffraction, and bending on entry is refraction.

The photoelectric effect is the one the wave model cannot account for. A wave would deliver energy to the metal continuously and spread over the whole surface, so a dim beam should still work — an electron would simply need to wait and gather enough. In practice nothing at all is emitted below a threshold frequency, however bright and however long you wait, and above it emission starts immediately even for very faint light.

That only makes sense if the energy arrives in indivisible packets of size $hf$: one packet, one electron, all or nothing.
distractorRationale: Interference is a wave effect — it depends on two paths adding or cancelling, which is what waves do.
Diffraction is a wave effect too, and its size depends on the wavelength.
Correct. The threshold frequency and the instant response cannot be explained by a wave delivering energy continuously.
Refraction follows from a wave changing speed between media, and the wave model predicts it correctly.

verification.justification: Interference, diffraction and refraction are all predicted by the wave model. Only the photoelectric effect requires quantised energy: the existence of a threshold frequency independent of intensity, and emission with no time lag at low intensity, both contradict continuous energy delivery.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / The photoelectric equation and work function
questions.stem: A metal surface has a work function of $2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$. Take the elementary charge as $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. Expressed in joules, the work function is
questions.solution:
One electronvolt is the energy an electron gains crossing a potential difference of one volt:
$$1\ \mathrm{eV}=e \times 1\ \mathrm{V}=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

So converting from electronvolts to joules means multiplying by $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$:
$$W=2.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}=3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

The electronvolt is the larger unit, so the number in joules is far smaller — a good sanity check on which way the conversion runs.
distractorRationale: Divided by $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ instead of multiplying, which converts the wrong way and gives an absurdly large energy.
Kept the number $2.0$ and simply attached $\times 10^{-19}$, without multiplying by $1.6$.
This is one electronvolt in joules. The work function is two of them.
Correct. $W=2.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}=3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / The photoelectric equation and work function
questions.stem: Light of frequency $6.0 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ falls on a metal whose work function is $2.0\ \mathrm{eV}$. Take $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$ and $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is
questions.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation is an energy account for one electron:
$$E_{k,\max}=hf-W.$$

The photon brings in $hf$; the work function $W$ is the toll paid to escape the surface; whatever remains is kinetic energy.

**Put both terms in joules first.** Mixing joules and electronvolts is the usual way this goes wrong.
$$hf=(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(6.0 \times 10^{14})=3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J},$$
$$W=2.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}=3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

**Subtract.**
$$E_{k,\max}=3.98 \times 10^{-19}-3.2 \times 10^{-19}=7.8 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

The photon only just clears the work function, so the electrons come out slowly. That is exactly what "just above the threshold" looks like.
distractorRationale: Correct. $E_{k,\max}=hf-W=3.98 \times 10^{-19}-3.2 \times 10^{-19}=7.8 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}$.
This is $hf$ alone. The work function still has to be paid before any kinetic energy is left over.
This is the work function alone, not what remains after it.
Added the two energies instead of subtracting. The escape cost reduces the electron's energy; it does not add to it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / The photoelectric equation and work function
questions.stem: A red laser is shone on a clean metal plate and no electrons are emitted. The laser is then replaced by one of the same colour but ten times brighter. What now happens?
options: $\text{Electrons are emitted, and each carries ten times more energy}$
$\text{Electrons are emitted, but only after a delay while energy builds up}$
$\text{Ten times as many electrons are emitted as before}$
questions.solution:
Emission is decided one photon at a time. A single photon either has enough energy to free a single electron, or it does not:
$$\text{emission requires } hf \ge W.$$

The colour is unchanged, so $f$ is unchanged, so $hf$ is unchanged. If it fell short before, it still falls short.

Brightness changes the **number** of photons arriving each second, not the energy of any one of them. Ten times as many photons that are each individually too weak is still nothing: an electron cannot save up two photons and spend them together.

So no electrons are emitted, no matter how bright the red laser is. The only way to get emission is to raise the frequency — to move towards the blue end of the spectrum.
distractorRationale: Brightness does not change photon energy. Only a higher frequency would, and the colour is the same.
Correct. $hf$ is unchanged and still below $W$, so nothing is emitted however bright the beam.
This is the wave-model prediction, and it is precisely what experiment contradicts. Energy does not accumulate; each absorption is a single all-or-nothing event.
Ten times zero is still zero. This answer would be right only if the original beam had emitted some electrons.

verification.justification: Emission requires hf >= W for a single photon. Intensity changes photon flux, not photon energy, so an unchanged frequency below threshold produces no emission at any intensity. This is the observation that rules out the classical energy-accumulation picture in option C.

questions.subject: physics
questions.syllabusRef: P-5 / Modern Physics / Photons and the Photoelectric Effect / The photoelectric equation and work function
questions.stem: A metal has a work function of $3.0\ \mathrm{eV}$. Take $h=6.63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\cdot s}$ and $e=1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. Below what frequency will this metal emit no electrons at all?
questions.solution:
The threshold is the frequency at which a photon has exactly enough energy to free an electron and none left over:
$$hf_{0}=W \ \Longrightarrow \ f_{0}=\frac{W}{h}.$$

**Convert the work function to joules first.**
$$W=3.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}=4.8 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}.$$

**Divide by $h$.**
$$f_{0}=\frac{4.8 \times 10^{-19}}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}=7.2 \times 10^{14}\ \mathrm{Hz}.$$

That sits just past the violet end of the visible range, so this metal would respond to ultraviolet but not to ordinary visible light.

The check worth running: a frequency has to come out large and positive. Anything negative, or with a negative exponent, means the division went the wrong way.
distractorRationale: Divided $h$ by $W$ rather than $W$ by $h$. That yields a time, not a frequency — and a frequency of $10^{-15}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ would be one oscillation every thirty million years.
This is the work function in joules, with the division by $h$ never carried out.
Used $e=1.0 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$ in the conversion instead of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$.
